meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Would Rather Have Two Girls at 21 Each Than One At 42'?
meta.ogDescription: Sung by W. C. Fields in 'You Can't Cheat an Honest Man' (1939) — but the gag was running in vaudeville by 1915, credited then to Great Lester.

answer.label: Sung by W. C. Fields — not his joke
answer.sourceLine: Fields really does sing this exact wording, about seventeen minutes into the 1939 Universal comedy You Can’t Cheat an Honest Man ↗, in a shower scene. But he did not write it: Quote Investigator’s ↗ earliest strong match is a Seattle vaudeville column of February 1915 crediting the ventriloquist Great Lester with “I would rather have two girls at 17 than one at 34.”
answer.confidenceText: Disputed origin — he sang it, he didn’t write it

source.excerpt:
“An optimist is a person who doesn’t give a whoop what happens so long as it doesn’t happen to him.” —Howard & McCane, Orpheum.
“I would rather have two girls at 17 than one at 34.” —Lester, Pantages.
trail: 1915 — The earliest strong match located by Quote Investigator ↗: a “Lines From Current Vaudeville” column in The Seattle Daily Times of 23 February 1915 logs “I would rather have two girls at 17 than one at 34” against “Lester, Pantages” — the ventriloquist Great Lester ↗. QI does not know whether he wrote it or lifted it.

1921–1922 — The gag keeps moving and keeps changing its arithmetic: a parody song title, “I’d Rather Have Two Girls at Sixteen Than One at Thirty-two,” in the Mt. Vernon Register-News of Illinois, then a reader’s submission — “I had rather have two girls 18 than one 36” — in the Greensboro Daily News, both documented by QI ↗.

1956 — Fred Allen prints the same 17/34 line in his memoir Much Ado About Me, page 102 ↗, among the jokes he copied into his first notebook when he switched from juggling to comedy. He gives no date for the notebook and makes no claim to the line.

1939 on screen — Fields sings the 21/42 form in You Can’t Cheat an Honest Man ↗, the Universal comedy whose story is credited to “Charles Bogle,” a Fields pen name; QI places it ↗ about seventeen minutes in, during the shower scene. From there it enters the Fields quote books — without a citation.
source.excerptNote: The 1915 column as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗: a newspaper simply logging the jokes then being told in local houses, each tagged with a performer and a theatre. Note the numbers — 17 and 34, not 21 and 42.

source.rightsNote: The exact 21/42 wording shown here is first documented in You Can’t Cheat an Honest Man (Universal Pictures, 1939) — a work published well after 1930, and treated here as in copyright. The older newspaper forms of the same gag (1915, 1921, 1922) are public domain, but they are not this wording: their numbers are 17/34, 16/32 and 18/36.

author.name: W. C. Fields
author.heading: The man who made it famous
author.bio: Born William Claude Dukenfield in Darby, Pennsylvania, Fields entered vaudeville in 1898 as a silent “tramp juggler” and only later let comedy take over the act. He wrote several of his own film stories under pen names — including Charles Bogle, the credited story writer on You Can’t Cheat an Honest Man, the 1939 picture in which this line appears. That double credit, performer and writer, is a large part of why lines he merely inherited from the vaudeville circuit are still filed under his name.

misattribution.heading: What actually gets misattributed here
misattribution.intro: The line travels as a Fields witticism. He did perform it — but he performed it as a vaudeville-trained comedian using vaudeville material, most of which nobody owned and nobody signed.

items.why: It was already circulating on the vaudeville stage: Quote Investigator’s ↗ earliest strong match is a February 1915 Seattle column, and QI concludes Fields — himself a vaudevillian from 1898 — may simply have heard it on the stage, calling him an important locus for its popularization rather than its source.

The arithmetic kept moving: 17 and 34 in 1915, 16 and 32 in an Illinois party report in 1921, 18 and 36 in a North Carolina reader’s column in 1922. QI ↗ notes the figure was variable; 21 and 42 is the form Fields sang on screen.
The collection printed the line as Fields’s and annotated a source for each quotation — but for this one, per QI ↗, the note named no movie, interview or book, carrying only a placeholder.

The line sits in the general quotes list with no source line attached ↗, immediately above an entry that is sourced to the 1939 film — so a reader scanning quickly can easily read the film credit onto the wrong line.

misattribution.truthLine: Fields sang it on screen in 1939; the same joke had already been printed in a Seattle vaudeville column in 1915, an Illinois social column in 1921 and a North Carolina jokes column in 1922, with only the arithmetic changing. Quote Investigator ↗ lays out the whole chain.

context.heading: A joke nobody owned
lead: Vaudeville ran on borrowed material. A gag that worked in Seattle on a Tuesday could be in another comedian’s notebook a week later, and nobody signed anything. This one surfaces in The Seattle Daily Times in February 1915, in a column headed “Lines From Current Vaudeville” that simply logged what was being told on local stages — the credit is a performer and a theatre, Lester, Pantages, and nothing more.

The loop closes neatly. Great Lester taught Edgar Bergen ↗ his ventriloquism; Bergen and Charlie McCarthy would go on to co-star with Fields ↗ in the 1939 Universal comedy where the joke resurfaces — Fields singing it while showering behind the circus tent, an elephant’s trunk for a showerhead ↗. Fields wrote that film’s story under his pen name Charles Bogle, which is likely why the line has read as his ever since.
context.detailsSummary: Why nobody can name the author
detailsBody: Quote Investigator is explicit about the limit of the evidence: it does not know whether Great Lester crafted the statement or lifted it from a fellow performer. A newspaper column recording what was being told on local stages is a snapshot of circulation, not a birth certificate — and QI notes the line was used by multiple comedians.

Fred Allen’s memoir shows the mechanism from the inside. Starting out, he stopped studying jugglers and started writing down other comedians’ lines; this one sits in his first notebook among a handful of stray gags he had heard. He never claimed it as his own, and never said when he wrote it down — QI can only place it, from context, somewhere between his 1911 high-school class and his 1914 monologue rewrite.

The Fields quote books inherited the problem rather than solving it. Drat! (1968) annotated a source for every line it printed; for this one, the note was the placeholder “To Come.” The 1970 Stanyan collection gave no precise citations at all.
context.pull: The numbers moved — 17, then 16, then 18, then 21. The joke never did.

Fields sang this exact wording about seventeen minutes into You Can’t Cheat an Honest Man (Universal Pictures, 1939), but he did not originate it: the earliest strong match is a “Lines From Current Vaudeville” column in The Seattle Daily Times, 23 February 1915, crediting the ventriloquist Great Lester with “I would rather have two girls at 17 than one at 34.” Quote Investigator calls Fields an important locus for the joke’s popularization rather than its source; the true author is not established.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the joke: earliest strong match is The Seattle Daily Times, 23 Feb 1915, page 9, 'Lines From Current Vaudeville', crediting 'Lester, Pantages' with 'I would rather have two girls at 17 than one at 34'; variants in the 1921 Mt. Vernon Register-News (sixteen/thirty-two) and 1922 Greensboro Daily News (18/36); Fields sang 'I'd rather have two girls at 21 each than one girl at 42' about 17 minutes into the 1939 film You Can't Cheat an Honest Man, in the shower; Fred Allen's Much Ado About Me (1956), p. 102 records the 17/34 form from his first notebook; Drat! (1968) gave the source note 'To Come'; the 1970 Stanyan collection gave no precise citations. QI concludes the origin is uncertain and Fields was a locus of popularization, not the author.

You Can't Cheat an Honest Man is a 1939 Universal Pictures comedy starring W. C. Fields, with Edgar Bergen (and Charlie McCarthy); the story is credited to 'Charles Bogle', a pen name used by W. C. Fields.

W. C. Fields was born William Claude Dukenfield (January 29, 1880 – December 25, 1946) in Darby, Pennsylvania; an American actor, comedian, juggler and writer; entered vaudeville in 1898 as a silent 'tramp juggler'; used the pen name 'Charles Bogle', credited on four of his 1930s films.

The Great Lester (born Maryan Czajkowski, 8 September 1878 – 14 July 1956) was a Polish-American vaudeville ventriloquist whose dummy was Frank Byron Jr.; the article states 'Edgar Bergen, one of the most famous ventriloquists of all time, was one of the Great Lester's pupils.'

This page describes the shower scene in You Can't Cheat an Honest Man as Fields appearing to walk naked through the circus after his bath 'with an elephant trunk as a showerhead', and gives the studio as Universal. (It does NOT mention the song lyric — that detail is sourced to Quote Investigator instead.)
